Be careful: if you have something that is a fast spreader, like English ivy, pachysandra, invasive forms of dead nettle or vinca/myrtle, please don’t spread this around your property and especially not near the property line where it could escape into woods or to your neighbors. (A note on the plant I was moving around which is White Nancy lamium/ spotted dead nettle (Lamium maculatum). It is not native to North America but is not known to be invasive. Plants behave differently in different locations. For example, I have Myrtle/vinca minor and it’s been very slow grower but it can spread into the woods and take over native plants in other locations so please be on the lookout for this and select something that will behave in your region and yard. 

No matter what, English ivy is a hard no. Nurseries need to stop selling that. 

Suggestions for ground cover welcome and please note if they’re native.

🍂 Fall is coming—don’t leave your garden unprepared!
The change of season is the perfect time to refresh, protect, and set the stage for a thriving garden next year. Here’s how:

🌱 Clean up spent plants to stop pests from overwintering
🌱 Refresh the soil with compost or organic matter
🌱 Plant cool-season crops like kale, spinach, and garlic
🌱 Protect perennials and shrubs with mulch and pruning
🌱 Support pollinators by leaving seed heads and brush piles
🌱 Care for your tools and lawn before frost hits

✨ Pro Tip: A little fall prep now means less stress and bigger rewards come spring.

June's to do list in the garden

We are now in winter, the leaves have fallen off the trees, and the garden is becoming dormant. It’s now time to prune the perennial plants in your garden. The perennial plants that have a woody stem will need to be pruned to reduce the size by about two thirds. Other herbaceous perennials that have a soft stem and often have a clumping base or multiple stems will need to be pruned right down to ground level.

Now is also the time to sow Rhodanthe everlasting daisy seeds. Sow seeds on the surface of prepared soil, they will germinate quickly with the arrival of winter rain and provide beautiful blooms that will attract all the best garden allies to your garden.  

Happy Gardening!

How to take Salvia Cuttings… 

I will say don’t panic if you have no stems yet for taking cuttings!  This was last year I actually have some salvias that haven’t even started flowering yet so I want to be keeping all the stems to myself!

This is the same method of how I take most my cuttings! Below a leaf node, remove lower leaves and chuck them in water!

For me personally if I do cuttings in compost they just fail because I forget about them 🤣

If I do my cuttings in a glass of water on my windowsill I can watch them root and then I sit there looking at them for months until I eventually pot them up! 🫣

It’s the best way to get free plants and you will have a lovely flowering plant ready for next year!

Charlies Winter Pruning Tips:🍂
“I like to give my deciduous trees and shrubs a really good prune as you can see the shape of the plant and pruning them is much easier without the weight of leaves. I was once told, if you can make a tree look good naked then come Spring, it can only look amazing.
Start by removing any crossing or rubbing branches. These cause wounds on the tree and infections can easily get into the plant so early removal is a bonus.
I then prune to shape, looking at where the plant will shoot from and prune according to the new growth it will put on come springtime.
When pruning larger branches, use a three-step cut system to prevent the bark from ripping. The first cut should be from the underside of the branch upwards and only about a third of the way through the branch.
The second cut from the top down, starting further out from the trunk than the first cut so when the branch breaks off it only rips to the point of the first cut. The third cut is the last cut closest to the trunk to tidy things up.”
Charlie Albone Richgro Brand Ambassador

Gardening Without the Pain 🌱

Gardening is a rewarding activity, but improper posture and repetitive movements can lead to back, neck, and knee pain. Studies show that bending, twisting, and lifting without proper form can strain your muscles and joints.

To keep your garden growing and pain-free, stretch before you start, lift with your legs, and take breaks to avoid overuse.

Happy gardening! 🌸
